Grey teal (Anas gracilis) hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C] after a development period of 25.25 days [ab = 25.25 days]. This incubation duration is typical for small-bodied dabbling ducks and reflects the careful thermal regulation provided by the attending adult. Newly hatched ducklings exhibit a mean wet body mass of 35 grams [Ww0 = 35 grams], a value that positions them within the expected range for precocial offspring that must rapidly become mobile. Upon emergence, these downy young are immediately capable of leaving the nest and foraging independently, although they remain under close parental protection for several weeks. The relatively modest investment in egg size, balanced against the extended developmental period, underscores a reproductive strategy common among Australasian waterfowl, where environmental conditions impose strong selection on both parental attendance and offspring viability immediately after hatching.

During the initial weeks of life, the growing juvenile Grey teal undergoes a critical developmental phase that culminates in the achievement of flight capability. Under the active thermal conditions typical of this species during periods of peak physiological activity, where body temperature is sustained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at approximately 56 days after hatching [tx = approximately 56 days after hatching]. This milestone, ranging between 50 and 55 days in many populations, marks the point at which the young bird can fly independently and begins to disperse from its natal area. The timing of fledging is intimately tied to the acquisition of sufficient muscle mass and feather development, processes that are heavily dependent on the availability of protein-rich aquatic invertebrate prey in the shallow wetlands the species frequents throughout the Australian and New Guinean regions.

The onset of reproductive capability in this species is characterized by a clear separation between physiological maturation and actual breeding activity. Puberty, defined as the achievement of functional gonadal maturation, is generally attained at 168 days after hatching [tp = 168 days after hatching] under sustained body temperatures averaging 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. However, despite this relatively early physiological capability, individuals do not typically engage in their first breeding attempt until considerably later. The time since birth at first brood is recorded as 1.4 years since birth [tR = 1.4 years since birth] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a delay that likely reflects the need for young birds to establish territories, secure breeding sites in seasonally fluctuating wetland environments, and accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation.

Adult body size in the Grey teal exhibits a modest but consistent sexual dimorphism, with females generally attaining a smaller ultimate wet weight than their male counterparts. The maximum adult body mass recorded for females is approximately 469 grams [Wwi = approximately 469 grams], whereas males commonly reach a larger ultimate wet weight of 508 grams [Wwi = 508 grams]. This difference, roughly 8%, is comparable to patterns observed in congeneric species such as the chestnut teal and is likely linked to the differential energetic investments associated with egg production in females versus the competitive demands of male-male interactions during the breeding season. The species' relatively small body size, combined with its high surface-area-to-volume ratio, necessitates a correspondingly elevated metabolic rate to sustain homeostasis, a feature that shapes its foraging ecology and habitat selection across its wide distribution.

Respirometry trials conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have characterized the basal metabolic demands of the Grey teal. When measured at a core body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum resting oxygen consumption rate reaches 599 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 599 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This comparatively high metabolic rate, typical of small-bodied Anatidae, underpins the species' capacity for sustained foraging and long-distance movements between ephemeral water bodies. In conjunction with this elevated energy demand, the species exhibits a modest reproductive output; females typically produce between 7 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 7 and 8 eggs per clutch], and only a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. This conservative reproductive rate is balanced by a notable maximum lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 31.5 years [am = approximately 31.5 years] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], demonstrating a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparity over high annual fecundity.
